summary: An extreme rainfall event on 2 July 2011 caused pluvial (surface-water) flooding in Copenhagen; the City's 2012 Cloudburst Management Plan puts the damage at DKK 5-6 bn, while the Climate-ADAPT case study says more than DKK 6bn. The City concluded the event showed that its earlier approach of storing rainwater in buffer areas was inadequate, and it responded with the 2012 Cloudburst Management Plan, which combines surface (green/blue) drainage with tunnels over a minimum 20-year timeframe.

interventions.title: Cloudburst Management Plan: combined surface (green/blue) drainage and tunnels
interventions.objective: Drain or store extreme stormwater at ground level (detention parks, green roads, roads with high kerbs leading water to flow routes) and use tunnels where surface drainage is not possible.
interventions.status_note: Adopted as a plan in 2012; Climate-ADAPT (2016) says the projects are 'only starting to be implemented now on a yearly basis'. Neither source reports completed outcomes.
prerequisites: public open space (parks, squares) available for temporary detention
street space for conveyance routes with raised kerbs
flow routes to a receiving water body (harbour/sea)
tunnel option where dense development leaves no surface space
coordination with the water utility and neighbouring municipalities
interventions.time_horizon: minimum 20-year plan (about 15 projects a year over 20-30 years per Climate-ADAPT)
constraints: Green and blue solutions are not suitable in densely built-up areas (plan p. 2).

Road owners decide whether projects are implemented; roads may need to be purchased, which requires cooperation between municipalities and private landowners (Climate-ADAPT, Success and limiting factors).
Stormwater needs treatment for water quality; solutions were still being tested (Climate-ADAPT, Success and limiting factors).
interventions.reported_outcome: Climate-ADAPT reports projections: the combined solution costs DKK 11bn at 2015 prices to build, with an expected overall benefit of DKK 5bn, and is about DKK 9bn better than a traditional sewer solution. The plan itself (2012) estimates construction costs up to 2033 at DKK 3.8 bn in present-day prices. These are cost-benefit projections, not observed results.
limitations: The plan states its calculations 'contain both technical and economic uncertainties' (p. 6).
The plan's 2012 cost estimate (DKK 3.8 bn) and Climate-ADAPT's 2015-price figure (DKK 11bn) differ; they come from different documents, bases and dates.
Earlier assumption that storage in buffer areas would suffice was found inadequate after 2 July 2011 (p. 7).
interventions.locator: p. 2 (Preface), p. 6 (Recommendations), p. 8 (section 3), p. 14 (20-year time frame); Climate-ADAPT sections Solutions and Costs and benefits

interventions.title: Risk-dimensioning service level: 100-year event, about 10 cm of water on streets
interventions.objective: Limit potentially damaging floods to those that statistically occur only once every 100 years, defining damaging as water levels reaching 10 cm on streets.
prerequisites: street and kerb design that keeps water away from basement entrances
constraints: The plan says protecting against events with return periods over 100 years would be disproportionately expensive compared with the resulting damage (p. 6).
interventions.reported_outcome: The plan's analyses found a negligible risk of water entering basement windows when water on roadways is kept at about 10 cm (p. 11). This is a modelled finding.
limitations: The plan notes that about 10 cm of water on roadways is likely to reduce passability during and after an event (p. 11).

summary: Heavy and very intense rainfall over southeast Queensland in the second week of January 2011 caused major river flooding in the Brisbane and Bremer Rivers. The Brisbane gauge peaked at 4.46 metres at 3:00am on 13 January 2011, the largest peak since January 1974 (5.45 metres). Inflows into Somerset and Wivenhoe dams were nearly double those of 1974, and a Queensland Floods Commission of Inquiry was announced on 17 January.

summary: The Camp Fire ignited at about 06:20 on 8 November 2018 near Camp Creek Road and Pulga Road in Butte County, California, and quickly reached the communities of Concow, Paradise and Magalia, triggering the evacuation of about 40,000 people. NIST reports 85 fatalities and more than 18,000 destroyed structures. Road closures and fire exposure complicated evacuation, and first responders set up 31 temporary refuge areas involving more than 1,200 civilians.

interventions.title: Collaborative evacuation planning with realistic, repeated training exercises (NIST R-EP 1 to R-EP 4)
interventions.objective: Develop evacuation plans with nearby first responder agencies, test them in realistic exercises that include fire, rescue, evacuation and traffic, and revise them using lessons from exercises and other WUI fires.
prerequisites: multi-agency coordination (fire, law enforcement, public works)
interventions.reported_outcome: Observed in the Camp Fire: an evacuation plan was in place and communicated before the incident (TF-EP 1), but it was designed for zoned/partial evacuation, not a complete simultaneous evacuation (TF-EP 3).
limitations: The plan assumed zoned/partial evacuation; the event required a near-simultaneous town-wide evacuation (TF-EP 3).
Egress arteries were closed by fire for long periods (68% of 08:00-14:15 had two or more of four arteries closed), limiting route-based evacuation.
interventions.locator: p. 225, section 14.1 (TF-EP 1, TF-EP 3, R-EP 1 to R-EP 4); also p. 40

interventions.title: Pre-planned, distributed wildfire safety zone system (NIST R-TRA 1 to R-TRA 7)
interventions.objective: When timely evacuation is not possible, give civilians reachable pre-planned wildfire safety zones whose number, size, distribution, access and maintenance account for fire exposure, fuel loads and population.
prerequisites: candidate open areas of adequate size (e.g. large parking lots, gravel areas, irrigated parks)
access pathways that avoid likely burnover locations
constraints: NIST notes the difficulty of reaching the Camelot Meadow Wild Fire Safety Zone and the need to place and maintain safety zones carefully (R-TRA 6).
interventions.reported_outcome: Observed during the incident: 31 ad hoc temporary refuge areas involving more than 1,200 civilians; consolidating TRAs and groups of civilians made management and evacuation easier (TF-TRA 12).
limitations: NIST states that ad hoc TRAs are by default a last resort and do not give the full benefit of a pre-planned system (p. 173/230). The TRAs used in the Camp Fire were improvised, not designated safe destinations.
This record does not treat TRAs as safe routing targets; NIST frames them as an emergency fallback when evacuation is not possible.

summary: The Cape Town Water Strategy describes a severe three-year drought from 2015 to 2017, which it calls a 1-in-590-year event. By March 2018 the supply dams had fallen to about one-fifth full. The city avoided 'Day Zero' by cutting water use by more than 40%, using restrictions, high drought tariffs and pressure management. Council approved a Water Strategy on 30 May 2019, committing to more than 300 million litres per day of new supply over ten years.

interventions.title: Network pressure management, leak detection and demand reduction during the crisis
interventions.objective: Reduce water demand and losses by controlling pressure zone by zone with smart controllers, plus leak detection and repairs.

interventions.reported_outcome: The strategy reports 102 zones isolated and optimised, saving over 50 million litres per day; together with a large water price increase, pressure management helped cut demand in February 2018 from 600 to 550 million litres per day.
limitations: The strategy states aggressive pressure management left some areas without water, sometimes for several hours, increasing complaints.

interventions.title: Escalating water restrictions and drought tariffs (crisis), then a simplified three-level restriction system (strategy)
interventions.objective: During the crisis: cut demand with restrictions and steeply higher tariffs. In the strategy: simplify to three restriction levels tied to indicative dam levels (below 80%, 70%, 60%), with an emergency response below 45%.
interventions.status_note: Crisis restrictions and the level-6B tariffs (February 2018) were implemented. The three-level system is a later strategy commitment (proposed).
prerequisites: legal authority to impose restrictions and tariffs
interventions.time_horizon: crisis 2017-2018; restriction levels reviewed annually under the strategy
constraints: Revenue-neutral tariff policy during restrictions put a financial burden on customers (strategy, 'Rainless day fund?' text box).
interventions.reported_outcome: Under level-6B tariffs from February 2018, the first block of the residential tariff rose more than six-fold to R30/kl. Use by billed residents fell from about 220 to about 120 litres per person per day, nearly 50% (strategy, Commitment 2).
limitations: The strategy reports residents found the many restriction levels confusing.
High bills from drought tariffs contributed to many complaints.

interventions.category: supply diversification (later strategy commitment, not a crisis action)
interventions.objective: Cost-effectively add groundwater, water reuse and desalination capacity to raise resilience and reduce the likelihood of severe restrictions, planning to 99.5% rather than 98% reliability.
prerequisites: desalination siting and environmental impact assessment
interventions.time_horizon: 10 years from strategy approval (2019); vision of a water-sensitive city by 2040

interventions.reported_outcome: Committed: more than 300 million litres per day over ten years at about R5,4 billion (2018 terms), plus about 70 million litres per day of demand-management savings. These are plan commitments, not results.
limitations: If 2015-2017 rainfall became the permanent norm, the strategy says the planned programme would meet only basic water needs and significant restrictions would remain until augmentation exceeds demand growth.
